CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should pursue active negotiations with the United States while maintaining its retaliatory tariffs as leverage. We should signal willingness to discuss structural issues like IP protection and market access, and offer increased purchases of US goods (especially agricultural and energy products) as a confidence-building measure, but resist any demands that would fundamentally undermine our industrial policy or state-led economic model. We should avoid further escalation while making clear we will not capitulate on core sovereignty issues.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not existential at this stage. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of US-China trade), with threats to cover the remaining $267 billion. China's exports to the US represent about 5% of GDP ($505 billion), making us more exposed in relative terms than the US (whose exports to China are ~0.7% of GDP). The RAND analysis notes the yuan has already depreciated 6% from 6.28 to 6.64 per dollar since April 2018, reflecting market stress. However, several factors mitigate the threat: (1) the US deliberately excluded consumer electronics like smartphones from tariffs to avoid hurting US consumers, meaning our highest-value exports are partially shielded; (2) as RAND notes, more than half the value of China's exports consists of components from other countries (South Korea, Japan), so tariffs also hurt US allies and supply chains; (3) China has already retaliated on $110 billion of $130 billion in US imports to China, covering nearly all US goods, and has strategically lowered tariffs on goods from other countries to redirect demand away from US suppliers. The Fox Business transcript confirms China has not yet tariffed US crude oil imports, preserving a significant bargaining chip. The Brookings analysis notes China is willing to buy more US products and open markets, and that it is unlikely Chinese leadership will 'cave in.' The negotiation posture is appropriate because: the US faces its own pain (soybean prices down 20%, Midwest farmers hurting, Boeing and auto sector exposed), creating domestic political pressure on Trump; the midterm elections have passed, reducing the political incentive for Trump to maintain maximum pressure; and a protracted trade war risks further yuan depreciation and export-sector unemployment in China's coastal manufacturing hubs. Negotiation allows us to offer purchase commitments that give Trump a face-saving 'win' while protecting our core industrial policy objectives.
key_factors: US tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports (~50% of bilateral trade), with threats to expand to nearly 100%
China's exports to US represent ~5% of GDP vs US exports to China at ~0.7% of GDP — asymmetric exposure
Yuan depreciated 6% (6.28 to 6.64/USD) since April 2018, reflecting currency pressure
US deliberately excluded consumer electronics (smartphones) from tariff lists to protect US consumers
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in US imports, nearly exhausting retaliatory capacity on goods
US soybean prices down 20%, Midwest agricultural sector under significant pressure
China strategically lowered tariffs on goods from other countries to redirect imports away from US
US crude oil not yet tariffed by China — preserved as leverage
Post-midterm political dynamics may create space for face-saving deal
More than half of China's export value consists of components from third countries (Japan, South Korea)

sources_cited.source_id: www.brookings.edu — Unpacked: The US-China Trade War
sources_cited.excerpt: U.S. exports to China are concentrated in agricultural products like soybeans, plus automobiles and Boeing aircraft sales. The trade war is already having an effect on those sectors. The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent.

sources_cited.source_id: www.rand.org — The U.S.-China Trade War: Different Messages
sources_cited.excerpt: $505 billion in potentially lost exports is a much larger slice of the Chinese economy (about 5 percent) than $130 billion is for the United States (about 0.7 percent). From early April, when the talk of trade wars began in earnest and the Chinese yuan was valued at 6.28 to the dollar, the currency has depreciated by 6 percent to 6.64 to the dollar as of July 6.

sources_cited.source_id: www.foxbusiness.com — The U.S.-China Trade War, Explained
sources_cited.excerpt: China has stated that Washington is 'putting a knife to China's neck and that China will not participate in the trade bullyism of the United States.' China also announced some tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods. This second round of Chinese tariffs is going to now cover $110 billion of the $130 billion of U.S.-China trade.

sources_cited.source_id: www.foxbusiness.com — US-China trade war: Why America must win
sources_cited.excerpt: China's middle class alone is expected to exceed the entire US population by 2022. The Council on Foreign Relations' August 2018 report outlines how China will provide hundreds of billions in subsidies and tax breaks, with state-controlled financial institutions providing low interest financing.
